extracted.intended_audience: policy scholars, law students, regulators, environmental advocates, and the general public interested in regulatory policy
extracted.subtask_description: Guidance and practices for influencing regulatory policy—especially environmental regulation—through economic analysis, litigation briefs, rulemaking comments, and public information. Emphasizes grounding arguments in facts and quantified economic metrics (e.g., social cost of carbon).

rubrics_metrics.name: Immersion in the facts
rubrics_metrics.description: ‘Immersion in the facts is often a way of quieting, and—more frequently than at least I would expect—a way of eliminating disagreement.’
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Use careful factual work and empirical evidence as the basis for policy arguments; examples include instances where the administration accepted regulations backed up by relevant facts. Anti-pattern: relying primarily on values or rhetoric without robust factual support.

rubrics_metrics.name: Ground regulations in solid cost–benefit analysis
rubrics_metrics.description: Regulations grounded in solid cost-benefit analysis are harder to undo and provide a stronger basis for defending public-health and environmental protections.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Ensure analyses credibly quantify benefits and costs so rulemakings can withstand political and legal challenges. Example: Policy Integrity’s mission centers on using cost–benefit to protect environment and health.

rubrics_metrics.name: Use economic analysis to support stronger protections
rubrics_metrics.description: Proponents of stronger environmental, public health, and safety protections should employ economic analysis rather than abandoning it, because avoiding economic analysis ceded discourse to opponents.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Produce rigorous economic arguments to counteract narratives that overestimate costs and underestimate benefits. Anti-pattern: refusing to use economic tools, which allows opponents to dominate public discourse.

rubrics_metrics.name: Accurately estimate and present costs and benefits
rubrics_metrics.description: Avoid overestimating costs and underestimating benefits; factual mis-estimation created a pathology in regulatory policy.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Carefully quantify and transparently report assumptions, ranges, and uncertainties in cost and benefit estimates; use best available science and methods to prevent bias in favor of arbitrary cost inflation.

rubrics_metrics.name: Quantify and apply the social cost of carbon
rubrics_metrics.description: Use the social cost of carbon (the dollar value of the damage a ton of CO2 emissions inflicts in a given year) in energy and regulatory decision-making.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Include SCC estimates in regulatory impact analyses and rulemaking comments; courts have considered briefs that address SCC (e.g., Seventh Circuit and Department of Energy energy-efficiency standards). Provide clear dollar-per-ton figures and methodology.

rubrics_metrics.name: Provide the public with accessible information to enable democratic demand
rubrics_metrics.description: Give people the information they need to demand, in a democracy, what they can get.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Make technical analyses and policy implications accessible to non-experts so citizens can engage and pressure decision-makers. Examples: public-facing briefs, summaries, and outreach accompanying technical reports.

rubrics_metrics.name: Intervene through focused amicus briefs in litigation
rubrics_metrics.description: Amicus briefs can shape high-stakes litigation and sometimes occupy significant oral-argument time; well-targeted briefs can establish important precedents.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Prepare briefs that address the core technical/legal issues the court lacks exposure to (e.g., extensive treatment of social cost of carbon). Anti-pattern: filing briefs that add little new factual or legal insight.

rubrics_metrics.name: Engage in state-level proceedings where expertise is limited
rubrics_metrics.description: State agencies often have less technical expertise than federal ones, creating opportunities to influence policy at the state level (e.g., electricity market structure, accounting for environmental benefits).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Target state proceedings with technical economic analysis and tailored recommendations; provide expertise to fill information gaps and shape state regulatory decisions.

rubrics_metrics.name: Train and integrate students as substantive contributors
rubrics_metrics.description: Students working in clinics function as colleagues who prepare amicus briefs and comments and serve as research assistants on policy projects.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Treat students as substantive contributors in drafting comments, briefs, and reports; clinics can be a pipeline to shape future regulatory practice and policy impact.
